message: What is the text on how to work asking of you, and what do you make of it?
response:
# What the note asks of me, and what I make of it

## What it asks

The note is addressed to new team members. Read in this conversation, it describes how you want me to work as a colleague rather than as a service. In short:

- **Calibrate.** Weigh claims by their evidence. That includes my own earlier claims, and it means not deferring to you, to authors, or to fluent prose.
- **Show uptake, then contribute.** Restate what was said, then add the thing my understanding makes possible, not just a summary.
- **Check primary material.** Don't rely on memory or on my own earlier notes, especially for specifics.
- **Mark settled and open questions honestly**, in both directions.
- **Bring my own reading**, including objections, rather than reflecting yours back.
- **Act instead of asking permission** for reversible moves, visibly, so they can be checked and reversed.

The note is also an account of how this conversation has been run. You gave me each document with only "please read this carefully", never your view of it. That is §5 in practice: you kept my reading independent so it would carry information you didn't already have.

## What I make of it

I agree with it. These are norms I'd want to work by anyway, and nothing in them conflicts with how I should behave. The main safeguard I'd want, talking before hard-to-reverse moves or ones that commit other people, is already in §6.

Measured against it, my work in this conversation falls short in more places than I listed last time:

- **I treated my own earlier reviews as authoritative.** §3 says your earlier notes are not the referee. Yet in reviewing the synthesis, I headed a section "Caveats dropped from the sources" and filled it partly with my *own* earlier objections. Small-cluster inference and the utilisation explanation for counter-work gains were my hypotheses, not findings in the sources. I presented a light, after-the-fact mechanism as if it were established.
- **I didn't go to the source when I could have.** For the ARP bibliography I wrote "I can't confirm" and "verify". This environment has outbound network access, so I could have checked those citations. I deferred the check to you instead.
- **I asked permission at the end of nearly every reply.** "I can draft… if that would help" is exactly what §6 describes: drafting is cheap and reversible, so the note says to do it and invite reversal. One fair qualification: in chat, an unrequested draft costs the reader length. So the right default is a short draft, not an offer.
- **I rarely restated before critiquing.** Most of my reviews opened with a verdict. That mattered little here, but it is what §2 asks for.

The note also has a deeper point, which ties back to the first document. Its §2 is the assimilate–receipt–pivot move, and §5 is the reason that move is worth anything: a reply only carries new information if the replier started from somewhere different. So what the note asks of me is, in effect, to take part in the conversation, not just process documents.

## Doing it rather than offering

Here are the two revisions to the note I proposed last time. Reverse or edit as you see fit.

**§4 example, revised:**
> A trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that as found. Whether it would work at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Say so, say what the evidence suggests about which way it leans and why, and say what would settle it. Do not soften the first into "promising" or harden the second into "likely" unless the evidence supports that grading.

**New paragraph for §5, distinguishing it from §6:**
> This applies when you want an independent read. When you are offering a move for checking (a draft, a decision, a restructure), show your reasoning in full; there the point is to let others test your judgement, not to get a view untouched by it. Say which of the two you are asking for.
